title: Miscellaneous Technical Amendments; Technical Amendment
content: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION Federal Aviation Administration 14 CFR Parts 1, 5, 13, 15, 16, 17, 21, 23, 25, 26, 27, 29, 31, 33, 34, 35, 38, 39, 43, 48, 61, 63, 65, 67, 71, 73, 77, 91, 95, 97, 99, 101, 103, 105, 110, 117, 120, 125, 133, 137, 150, 151, 152, 153, 155, 156, 157, 158, 161, 169, 170, 171, 183, 185, 187, 189, 193, 198, and 450 [Docket No.: FAA-2026-4853; Amdt. Nos. 1-81, 5-3, 13-41, 15-5, 16-2, 17-2, 21-111, 23-66, 25-154, 26-8, 27-52, 29-60, 31-6, 33-37, 34-8, 35-11, 38-2, 39-20000, 43-65, 48-4, 61-162, 63-49, 65-68, 67-24, 71-59, 73-10, 77-14, 91-386, 95-341, 97-1341, 99-17, 101-12, 103-18, 105-14, 110-4, 117-2, 120-5, 125-79, 133-17, 137-19, 150-5, 151-40, 152-14, 153-2, 155-3, 156-2, 157-8, 158-5, 161-3, 169-4, 170-5, 171-18, 183-19, 185-4, 187-37, 189-5, 193-2, 198-5, 450-5] RIN 2120-AM11 Miscellaneous Technical Amendments; Technical Amendment AGENCY: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation (DOT). ACTION: Final rule; technical amendment. SUMMARY: This technical amendment contains non-substantive corrections to address typographical errors, editorial errors, and outdated or incorrect references in various parts of FAA regulations. DATES: Effective November 23, 2026. ADDRESSES: For information on where to obtain copies of rulemaking documents and other information related to this final rule, see “Additional Information” in the SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION section of this document. FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Jesse Holston, Office of Rulemaking, ARM-200, Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Ave. SW, Washington, DC 20591; email: jesse.c.holston@faa.gov. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: I. Authority for This Rulemaking and Good Cause for Immediate Adoption A. Authority for This Rulemaking FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety is found in title 49 of the United States Code (U.S.C.). Subtitle I, section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of FAA's authority. This rulemaking is issued under the authority described in subtitle I, section 106(f), which establishes the Administrator's authority to promulgate and revise regulations and rules related to aviation safety. This regulation is within the scope of that authority. The Commercial Space Launch Act of 1984, as amended and codified at 51 U.S.C. 50901-50923 (the Act), authorizes the Secretary of Transportation to oversee, license, and regulate commercial launch and reentry activities, and the operation of launch and reentry sites within the United States or as carried out by U.S. citizens. Section 50905 directs the Secretary to exercise this responsibility consistent with public health and safety, safety of property, and the national security and foreign policy interests of the United States. In addition, section 50903 requires the Secretary to encourage, facilitate, and promote commercial space launches and reentries by the private sector. As codified in 49 CFR 1.83(b), the Secretary has delegated authority to the FAA Administrator to carry out these functions. B. Good Cause for Immediate Adoption Section 553(b) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (5 U.S.C.) authorizes agencies to dispense with notice and comment procedures for rules when the agency for “good cause” finds that those procedures are “impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” Under this section, an agency, upon finding good cause, may issue a final rule without seeking comment prior to the rulemaking. In addition, the APA requires agencies to delay the effective date of regulations for 30 days after publication, unless the agency finds good cause to make the regulations effective sooner. See, 5 U.S.C. 553(d). This rulemaking action makes technical amendments that affect the clarity of existing regulations. These amendments will not impose any additional substantive restrictions or requirements on the persons affected by these regulations. Because this action merely makes technical amendments, FAA finds notice and public comment under 5 U.S.C. 553(b) to be unnecessary. For the same reason, FAA finds good cause exists under 5 U.S.C. 553(d) for making this rule effective in less than 30 days. II. Technical Amendments FAA is making technical amendments to parts 1, 5, 13, 15, 16, 17, 21, 23, 25, 26, 27, 29, 31, 33, 34, 35, 38, 39, 43, 48, 61, 63, 65, 67, 71, 73, 77, 91, 95, 97, 99, 101, 103, 105, 110, 117, 120, 125, 133, 137, 150, 151, 152, 153, 155, 156, 157, 158, 161, 169, 170, 171, 183, 185, 187, 189, 193, 198, and 450 of those regulations found in title 14, Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR). All amendments are non-substantive and correct typographical errors, editorial errors, and outdated or incorrect references. The following is a summary of the various amendments to each of the above-listed parts. Chapter 1 The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 amended 49 U.S.C. 106 by removing the language previously within subsection (g), modifying it, and moving the modified text to subsection (f). 1 In addition, the Act designated subsection (g) as reserved. 2 As a result, section 106(g) no longer provides authority for Chapter 1. Prior to the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, section 106(g) established the Administrator's authority to promulgate and revise regulations and rules related to aviation safety; this authority is now found in section 106(f). To implement this statutory change, this rule revises the authority citation for parts 13, 15, 16, 26, 31, 33, 34, 38, 39, 77, 95, 99, 103, 105, 117, 133, 137, 150, 151, 152, 153, 155, 156, 157, 158, 161, 169, 170, 171, 185, 189, 193, and 198 by removing the reference to 49 U.S.C. 106(g) and adding a reference to 49 U.S.C. 106(f). In addition, this rule revises the authority citation for parts 5, 23, 25, 27, 29, 35, 48, 71, 73, 97, 101, 110, 125, 183, and 187 by removing the reference to 49 U.S.C. 106(g). No further changes are needed to these authority citations as they already include a reference to 106(f). 1 See Public Law 118-63, Sec. 204. 2 See Public Law 118-63, Sec. 204(b). Part 1 In § 1.1, Military operations area, the word “theses” is removed and replaced with “these” to correct a typographical error. Part 13 Sections 13.43(c) and 13.210(c) are amended to remove the addresses for filing a document with the FAA Hearing Docket. The address is replaced with a website where a filer may find the most up to date addresses for filing. These changes allow FAA to provide the most current address information for filing. Part 17 Sections 17.15(b), 17.27(b), and 17.59(b) are amended to remove the addresses for filing and replace it with a website where a filer may find the most up to date addresses for filing. These changes allow FAA to provide the most current address information for filing. Part 21 On September 3, 2025, FAA published the final rule titled “Falsification, Reproduction, Alteration, Omission, or Incorrect Statements.” This rule amended, restructured, and consolidated the falsification regulations presently located throughout title 14 of the CFR; however, it inadvertently overwrote the authority citation for parts 21 and 61. This amendment changes the authority for parts 21 and 61 back to what was in place prior to publication of the Falsification final rule. Part 29 Section 29.1337(e)(1), which concerns rotor drive system transmissions and gearboxes that utilize ferromagnetic materials, is amended to remove an incorrect cross reference. Section 29.1305(a)(22), which concerns fuel pump failure indicators, is removed and replaced with § 29.1305(a)(23), which discusses ferromagnetic chip detector devices and indicator respectively. Part 43 In part 43 appendix A, paragraph (c)(31), the word “and” is removed and replaced with “an” in the last sentence of the paragraph. This change corrects a typographical error. Part 61 As previously stated, FAA's final rule, “Falsification, Reproduction, Alteration, Omission, or Incorrect Statements,” inadvertently overwrote the authority citation for parts 21 and 61. This amendment changes the authority for part 61 back to what was in place prior to publication of the Falsification final rule. The phrase “Aeromedical Certification Branch” is removed from § 61.29(e) and replaced with “Aerospace Medical Certification Division” to reflect organizational changes in FAA. On July 24, 2025, FAA published the final rule, “Modernization of Special Airworthiness Certification (MOSAIC),” which updated regulations governing the manufacture, certification, operation, maintenance, and alteration of light-sport aircraft. To maintain consistency after removing the “light-sport aircraft” definition from § 1.1 and its references in subpart J, the rule eliminated related mentions throughout the regulations. Since publication, FAA has identified five remaining instances of the term “light-sport aircraft” in parts 61 and 65 that still require replacement. The revisions to part 61 are as follows: • Section 61.411(b)(2): This revision was omitted from the amendatory instructions inadvertently when publishing the final rule. In this section, the term “a light-sport aircraft” is replaced with “an aircraft meeting the performance limits and design requirements of § 61.316.” • Section 61.415 introductory text: This revision was omitted from the amendatory instruction inadvertently when publishing the final rule. In this section, the term “a light-sport aircraft” is replaced with “an aircraft meeting the performance limits and design requirements of § 61.316.” • Section 61.415(f): Although this revision was included in Amendatory Instruction No. 57 in the final rule, the change was not made. In this section, the term “light-sport aircraft” is replaced with “aircraft.” • Section 61.415(g): Although this revision was included in Amendatory Instruction No. 57 in the final rule, the change was not made. In this section, the term “light-sport aircraft” is replaced with “aircraft.” Part 63 The phrase “Aeromedical Certification Branch” is removed from § 63.16(f) and replaced with “Aerospace Medical Certification Division” to reflect organizational changes in FAA. Part 65 In § 65.16(d), references to “telegram” as a way to request a temporary certification confirmation for a lost certificate issued under part 65 or a medical certificate are removed to align with the agency's current practice 3 and modernized systems. Thus, this technical amendment updates all references to “telegram” in this paragraph by removing and replacing it with either “document” or “in a form and manner acceptable to the Administrator.” 3 See FAA Order 8900.1, Vol. 5, Ch. 5, Sec. 1, Chg. 1013. FAA's final rule, “Modernization of Special Airworthiness Certification (MOSAIC),” updated regulations governing the manufacture, certification, operation, maintenance, and alteration of light-sport aircraft. To maintain consistency after removing the “light-sport aircraft” definition from § 1.1 and align repairman certificate (light-sport) holder privileges with the expansion of aircraft categories eligible for light-sport category airworthiness certificates, the title of the repairman certificate was revised to repairman certificate (light-sport). Since publication, FAA has identified § 65.101(b) was inadvertently omitted from the amendatory instructions when publishing the final rule. In this section, the term “light-sport aircraft” is replaced with “light-sport.” Part 67 The phrase “Aeromedical Certification Division” is removed from §§ 67.401, 67.407, and 67.409, and is replaced with “Aerospace Medical Certification Division” to reflect organizational changes in FAA. Part 73 In § 73.19(a), “Airspace Policy Group” is replaced with “Rules and Regulations Group” to reflect organizational changes in FAA. Part 91 In §§ 91.225 (d)(5) and 91.511(f), “Gulf of Mexico” is replaced with “Gulf of America” to align with Executive Order 14172, “Restoring Names that Honor American Greatness.” Part 120 Part 120 has multiple references to “Antidrug and Alcohol Misuse Prevention Program,” which is outdated terminology in the Operations Specification that is no longer used by industry or FAA. All instances of this term are replaced with “Drug and Alcohol Testing Program.” Part 450 In § 450.117 (d)(4), a comma is added between “position” and “velocity” to separate the terms. This corrects a typographical error. III. Regulatory Notices and Analyses A. Regulatory Impact Analysis Executive Order (E.O.) 12866 (“Regulatory Planning and Review”) and E.O. 13563 (“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) require agencies to regulate in the “most cost-effective manner,” to make a “reasoned determination that the benefits of the intended regulation justify its costs,” and to develop regulations that “impose the least burden on society.” The Office of Management and Budget has determined this rule is not a significant regulatory action as defined in E.O. 12866. This rule involves non-substantive technical amendments. FAA does not expect there will be any additional costs conferred on the public or the Federal Government because none of the technical and editorial changes included in this rule will change existing regulatory requirements. FAA anticipates minor administrative cost savings due to efficiencies for both industry and FAA by eliminating outdated language. B. Regulatory Flexibility Act The Regulatory Flexibility Act, 5 U.S.C. 601, et seq., as amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (Pub. L. 104-121), requires an agency to prepare and make available to the public a regulatory flexibility analysis that describes the effect of the rule on small entities ( i.e., small businesses, small organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions). A regulatory flexibility analysis is not required when a rule is exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking. C. International Trade Impact Assessment The Trade Agreements Act of 1979 (Pub. L. 96-39), as amended by the Uruguay Round Agreements Act (Pub. L. 103-465), prohibits Federal agencies from establishing standards or engaging in related activities that create unnecessary obstacles to the foreign commerce of the United States. Pursuant to these Acts, the establishment of standards is not considered an unnecessary obstacle to the foreign commerce of the United States, so long as the standard has a legitimate domestic objective, such as the protection of safety and does not operate in a manner that excludes imports that meet this objective. The statute also requires consideration of international standards and, where appropriate, that they be the basis for U.S. standards. FAA has assessed the potential effect of this rule and determined it is in accord with the Trade Agreements Act as the rule applies equally to domestic and foreign persons engaged in aviation activities under 14 CFR. As previously discussed, this rulemaking corrects several technical errors that affect the clarity of the regulatory text. These corrections do not impose any additional restrictions or requirements on the persons affected by these regulations. D. Unfunded Mandates Assessment The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (2 U.S.C. 1531-1538) governs the issuance of Federal regulations that require unfunded mandates. An unfunded mandate is a regulation that requires a State, local, or Tribal government or the private sector to incur direct costs without the Federal Government having first provided the funds to pay those costs. FAA determined the rule will not result in the expenditure of $187,000,000 or more ($100,000,000 adjusted for inflation using the most current Implicit Price Deflator for the Gross Domestic Product) by State, local, or Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or the private sector, in any one year. E. Paperwork Reduction Act The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3507(d)) requires FAA to consider the impact of paperwork and other information collection burdens imposed on the public. FAA has determined there is no new requirement for information collection associated with this final rule. F. International Compatibility In keeping with U.S. obligations under the Convention on International Civil Aviation, it is FAA policy to conform to International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Standards and Recommended Practices to the maximum extent practicable. FAA has determined there are no ICAO Standards and Recommended Practices that correspond to these regulations. G. Environmental Analysis FAA has analyzed the environmental impacts of this final rule pursuant to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) (42 U.S.C. 4321, et seq. ). FAA has determined this rule is categorically excluded pursuant to FAA Order 1050.1G. Categorical exclusions are categories of actions FAA has determined normally do not significantly affect the quality of the human environment and therefore do not require either an environmental assessment (EA) or environmental impact statement (EIS). In analyzing the applicability of a categorical exclusion, FAA must also consider whether extraordinary circumstances are present that would warrant the preparation of an EA or EIS. This rulemaking, which contains technical amendments meant to address typographical errors, editorial errors, and outdated or incorrect references in various parts of FAA regulations, is categorically excluded pursuant to FAA Order 1050.1G, Appendix B, Paragraph B-2.6(f), which categorically excludes issuance of regulatory documents. FAA does not anticipate any environmental impacts, and there are no extraordinary circumstances present in connection with this rulemaking. IV. Executive Order Determinations A. Executive Order 13132, Federalism FAA has analyzed this final rule under the principles and criteria of E.O. 13132, Federalism. FAA has determined that this action will not have a substantial direct effect on the States, or the relationship between the Federal Government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government, and, therefore, will not have federalism implications. B. Executive Order 13175, Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments Consistent with E.O. 13175, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, 4 and FAA Order 1210.20, American Indian and Alaska Native Tribal Consultation Policy and Procedures, 5 FAA ensures that Federally Recognized Tribes (Tribes) are given the opportunity to provide meaningful and timely input regarding proposed Federal actions that have the potential to have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes; or to affect uniquely or significantly their respective Tribes. At this point, FAA has not identified any unique or significant effects, environmental or otherwise, on Tribes resulting from this final rule. 4 65 FR 67249 (Nov. 6, 2000). 5 FAA Order No. 1210.20 (Jan. 28, 2004), available at: www.faa.gov/documentLibrary/media/1210.pdf. C. Executive Order 13211, Regulations That Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use FAA analyzed this final rule under E.O. 13211, Actions Concerning Regulations that Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use (May 18, 2001). FAA has determined it is not a “significant energy action” under the E.O. and is not likely to have a significant adverse effect on the supply, distribution, or use of energy. D. Executive Order 13609, Promoting International Regulatory Cooperation E.O. 13609, Promoting International Regulatory Cooperation, promotes international regulatory cooperation to meet shared challenges involving health, safety, labor, security, environmental, and other issues and to reduce, eliminate, or prevent unnecessary differences in regulatory requirements. FAA has analyzed this action under the policies and agency responsibilities of E.O. 13609 and has determined this action will have no effect on international regulatory cooperation. E. Executive Order 14192, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation This rule is an E.O. 14192 deregulatory action because it has total costs less than zero as it removes outdated language and removes related minor administrative burdens. V. Additional Information A. Electronic Access and Filing A copy of this final rule and all background material may be viewed online at www.regulations.gov using the docket number listed above. Electronic retrieval help and guidelines are available on the website. It is available 24 hours each day, 365 days each year. An electronic copy of this document may also be downloaded from the Office of the Federal Register's website at www.federalregister.gov and the Government Publishing Office's website at www.govinfo.gov. A copy may also be found at FAA's Regulations and Policies website at www.faa.gov/regulations_policies. Copies may also be obtained by sending a request to the Federal Aviation Administration, Office of Rulemaking, ARM-1, 800 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20591, or by calling (202) 267-9677. Requesters must identify the docket or notice number of this rulemaking. All documents FAA considered in developing this final rule, including economic analyses and technical reports, may be accessed in the electronic docket for this rulemaking. B. Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act The Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA) of 1996 (Pub. L. 104-121) requires FAA to comply with small entity requests for information or advice about compliance with statutes and regulations within its jurisdiction. A small entity with questions regarding this document may contact its local FAA official, or the person listed under the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT heading at the beginning of the preamble. To find out more about SBREFA on the internet, visit www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/rulemaking/sbre_act/.
